messages.author: d290713b7d428392
messages.subject: Error in running AMOVA
parts:
Hello everyone

I am working on SNP dataset of 346 individuals. While running AMOVA, I came across the following error:

In poppr.amova(Rufi2771genind, ~Ind/Country/Pop) :
  Data with mixed ploidy or ambiguous allele dosage cannot have within-individual variance calculated until the dosage is correctly estimated.

 This function will return the summary statistic, rho (Ronfort et al 1998) but be aware that this estimate will be skewed due to ambiguous dosage. If you have zeroes encoded in your data, you may wish to remove them.
 To remove this warning, use within = FALSE

Please let me know how can I overcome this error.

Thank You
Palvi Malik

messages.author: d192ec4b1d416345
messages.subject: Re: [poppr] Error in running AMOVA
parts:
Hi Palvi,

See my answers below:

Since, I had no hierarchy in my data, just 346 samples assigned to five sub-populations, I am interpreting the results as variation between sub-populations to be 62.81224 and within sub-populations to be 521.89040. I don't understand phi output. Can you please helo me?

The phi output is the differentiation statistic. In general, the higher this number is, the higher the differentiation between populations. A few years ago, I wrote a short primer on AMOVA (https://grunwaldlab.github.io/Population_Genetics_in_R/AMOVA.html), but there are also many other sources that talk a bit more in depth about the specific interpretations and caveats: http://userwww.sfsu.edu/efc/classes/biol710/amova/amova.htm.

That being said, your output does not match what I would expect from the input code. By default, poppr.amova will calculate within-individual variance, so you should have the following variances:

Between Pop
Between samples Within Pop
Within samples
Total

The Phi result you have right now thus is the rho summary statistic. This article talks about the statistic in a modern context: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fevo.2018.00066/full

Also, I could not understand how to set strata in data.I understood rest of the code except:
strata(Rufi2771genind) <- pop.data[match(indNames(Rufi2771genind), pop.data$Ind), ]
 I am working on a couple of populations, so I need to use this function time and again. Can you please clarify it more. 

The strata is a way to keep all of your population definitions in one place. You can read a tutorial on it here: https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/raw/master/tutorials/tutorial-strata.pdf

You should only need to use this command once per data set to store the population strata. From there, you can use the setPop() function to set the population of the data set to a given column or set of columns in the strata. For example, if you imported the attached data set and used that as your strata, you would set the population to the PROGRAM column using setPop(Rufi2771genind) <- ~PROGRAM

To get specifically to the command I provided, this does two things:

1. It ensures that the strata are in the same order as the data by subsetting (using the square brackets) the "pop.data" data frame with the result of the "match()" function, which will gives the correct arrangement of pop.data$Ind compared to the individual names in the genind object.

2. It assigns the data frame pop.data to be the source of population strata in your genind object. 

I hope that helps.

Best
Zhian

On Fri, Sep 21, 2018 at 9:38 PM Zhian Kamvar <zka...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi,

There are two things I can address here:

1. (SOLUTION) This is a similar problem to a post from earlier this month: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/poppr/TDOs4sAHADU/iYBO9H6ZEQAJ
The hierarchy is specified from the broadest to the narrowest: (e.g. population/subpopulation/subsubpopulation). However, the result you are getting is because you are specifying "Ind" as a hierarchical level.

2. There's a lot of unnecessary code in what you posted. You should only need 5 lines. I've corrected them and added comments (and changed the names of some of the variables for consistency.

Rufi2771vcf <- read.vcfR("OnlyRufi2771.vcf") # read in VCF file
Rufi2771genind <- vcfR2genind(Rufi2771vcf) # convert VCF to genind
pop.data <- read.table("trial_popfile.txt", sep = "\t", header = TRUE) # read in population strata
strata(Rufi2771genind) <- pop.data[match(indNames(Rufi2771genind), pop.data$Ind), ] # add population strata to genind, making sure the names match
Rufi2771amova <- poppr.amova(Rufi2771genind, ~Pop, clonecorrect = TRUE) # perform AMOVA testing structure of Pop

Hope that helps,
Zhian

On Wednesday, September 26, 2018 at 5:03:40 AM UTC-4, Zhian Kamvar wrote:
Hi Palvi,

See my answers below:

Since, I had no hierarchy in my data, just 346 samples assigned to five sub-populations, I am interpreting the results as variation between sub-populations to be 62.81224 and within sub-populations to be 521.89040. I don't understand phi output. Can you please helo me?

The phi output is the differentiation statistic. In general, the higher this number is, the higher the differentiation between populations. A few years ago, I wrote a short primer on AMOVA (https://grunwaldlab.github.io/Population_Genetics_in_R/AMOVA.html), but there are also many other sources that talk a bit more in depth about the specific interpretations and caveats: http://userwww.sfsu.edu/efc/classes/biol710/amova/amova.htm.

That being said, your output does not match what I would expect from the input code. By default, poppr.amova will calculate within-individual variance, so you should have the following variances:

Between Pop
Between samples Within Pop
Within samples
Total

The Phi result you have right now thus is the rho summary statistic. This article talks about the statistic in a modern context: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fevo.2018.00066/full

Also, I could not understand how to set strata in data.I understood rest of the code except:
strata(Rufi2771genind) <- pop.data[match(indNames(Rufi2771genind), pop.data$Ind), ]
 I am working on a couple of populations, so I need to use this function time and again. Can you please clarify it more. 

The strata is a way to keep all of your population definitions in one place. You can read a tutorial on it here: https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/raw/master/tutorials/tutorial-strata.pdf

You should only need to use this command once per data set to store the population strata. From there, you can use the setPop() function to set the population of the data set to a given column or set of columns in the strata. For example, if you imported the attached data set and used that as your strata, you would set the population to the PROGRAM column using setPop(Rufi2771genind) <- ~PROGRAM

To get specifically to the command I provided, this does two things:

1. It ensures that the strata are in the same order as the data by subsetting (using the square brackets) the "pop.data" data frame with the result of the "match()" function, which will gives the correct arrangement of pop.data$Ind compared to the individual names in the genind object.

2. It assigns the data frame pop.data to be the source of population strata in your genind object. 

I hope that helps.

Best
Zhian

On Fri, Sep 21, 2018 at 9:38 PM Zhian Kamvar <zka...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi,

There are two things I can address here:

1. (SOLUTION) This is a similar problem to a post from earlier this month: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/poppr/TDOs4sAHADU/iYBO9H6ZEQAJ
The hierarchy is specified from the broadest to the narrowest: (e.g. population/subpopulation/subsubpopulation). However, the result you are getting is because you are specifying "Ind" as a hierarchical level.

2. There's a lot of unnecessary code in what you posted. You should only need 5 lines. I've corrected them and added comments (and changed the names of some of the variables for consistency.

Rufi2771vcf <- read.vcfR("OnlyRufi2771.vcf") # read in VCF file
Rufi2771genind <- vcfR2genind(Rufi2771vcf) # convert VCF to genind
pop.data <- read.table("trial_popfile.txt", sep = "\t", header = TRUE) # read in population strata
strata(Rufi2771genind) <- pop.data[match(indNames(Rufi2771genind), pop.data$Ind), ] # add population strata to genind, making sure the names match
Rufi2771amova <- poppr.amova(Rufi2771genind, ~Pop, clonecorrect = TRUE) # perform AMOVA testing structure of Pop

Hope that helps,
Zhian

messages.subject: Re: [poppr] Error in running AMOVA
parts:
Hello all,

We've been able to determine that this behavior was due to a corner case where vcfR created a genind object where the alleles were represented as 0 and 1. In a few functions (including AMOVA), poppr treats zeroes differently to handle individuals with mixed or ambiguous ploidy, which is why Palvi was getting the warning posted earlier.

The solution here was to use vcfR2genlight instead of vcfR2genind.

Cheers,
Zhian

The Phi result you have right now thus is the rho summary statistic. This article talks about the statistic in a modern context: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fevo.2018.00066/full

Also, I could not understand how to set strata in data.I understood rest of the code except:
strata(Rufi2771genind) <- pop.data[match(indNames(Rufi2771genind), pop.data$Ind), ]
 I am working on a couple of populations, so I need to use this function time and again. Can you please clarify it more. 

The strata is a way to keep all of your population definitions in one place. You can read a tutorial on it here: https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/raw/master/tutorials/tutorial-strata.pdf

You should only need to use this command once per data set to store the population strata. From there, you can use the setPop() function to set the population of the data set to a given column or set of columns in the strata. For example, if you imported the attached data set and used that as your strata, you would set the population to the PROGRAM column using setPop(Rufi2771genind) <- ~PROGRAM

To get specifically to the command I provided, this does two things:

1. It ensures that the strata are in the same order as the data by subsetting (using the square brackets) the "pop.data" data frame with the result of the "match()" function, which will gives the correct arrangement of pop.data$Ind compared to the individual names in the genind object.

2. It assigns the data frame pop.data to be the source of population strata in your genind object.

Hi,

There are two things I can address here:

1. (SOLUTION) This is a similar problem to a post from earlier this month: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/poppr/TDOs4sAHADU/iYBO9H6ZEQAJ
The hierarchy is specified from the broadest to the narrowest: (e.g. population/subpopulation/subsubpopulation). However, the result you are getting is because you are specifying "Ind" as a hierarchical level.

2. There's a lot of unnecessary code in what you posted. You should only need 5 lines. I've corrected them and added comments (and changed the names of some of the variables for consistency.

Rufi2771vcf <- read.vcfR("OnlyRufi2771.vcf") # read in VCF file
Rufi2771genind <- vcfR2genind(Rufi2771vcf) # convert VCF to genind
pop.data <- read.table("trial_popfile.txt", sep = "\t", header = TRUE) # read in population strata
strata(Rufi2771genind) <- pop.data[match(indNames(Rufi2771genind), pop.data$Ind), ] # add population strata to genind, making sure the names match
Rufi2771amova <- poppr.amova(Rufi2771genind, ~Pop, clonecorrect = TRUE) # perform AMOVA testing structure of Pop

Hope that helps,
